description: A single-panel grayscale electron micrograph, labelled "(e)" in its top-left corner, with a black 200 nm scale bar in a white box at the bottom-left. There are no axes, no legend, no colour scale and no numeric annotations: the only printed text is the panel letter "(e)" and the scale-bar value "200 nm". The field of view shows a finely mottled, low-contrast matrix with a faintly wavy or tweed-like texture, within which many very bright, nanometre-scale speckles are dispersed, together with a smaller number of slightly larger bright features a few tens of nanometres across and a few short bright curved segments near the upper-right. The rendering is grainy and slightly blurred, so individual particle shapes and sizes cannot be measured reliably, and nothing in the panel identifies the phase responsible. Resolution of the pixels alone cannot separate TEM from high-magnification SEM here; the TEM assignment rests on the 200 nm scale bar. Taken by itself the panel demonstrates only that the material contains a dense dispersion of bright nanoscale contrast features in an otherwise microstructurally rather uniform matrix, consistent with the fine-scale precipitate population discussed in the paper, but no phase identity, composition or size value can be read from it.

observations.observation: The supplied figure is a single grayscale micrograph panel, labelled '(e)' in the top-left corner, with no accompanying panels.
A black scale bar in a white box at the bottom-left is labelled '200 nm'.
The panel carries no axes, no legend, no colour scale and no numeric annotations other than the panel letter and the scale-bar value.
The imaged region consists of a finely mottled, low-contrast matrix with a faint wavy/tweed-like texture, not a clearly resolved grain or lamellar structure.
Numerous very bright nanometre-scale speckles are dispersed throughout the matrix, appearing brighter than the surrounding mottled background.
A small number of somewhat larger bright features and short bright curved segments are visible, mainly toward the upper-right of the field of view.
The image is grainy and slightly blurred, so individual particle shapes, sizes and area fractions cannot be measured from the pixels.
No phase name, composition, processing condition or sample identifier is printed anywhere in this panel.
The 200 nm scale bar indicates the field of view spans roughly one micrometre across, i.e. a sub-micrometre/nanoscale imaging length scale.
